subject: history
displayName: KS3 History — Civil Rights, Protest & Social Change
subtitle: The American Civil Rights Movement, anti-apartheid struggle, and protest movements in modern history.

data.targetWord: the rights people have as equal citizens, including the right to vote, use public services, and be treated fairly by the law

examples.en-GB: Civil rights campaigners fought for equal access to education, transport and voting.

data.targetWord: the forced separation of people by race, enforced by law and custom in the southern United States

examples.en-GB: Segregation required Black and white people to use separate schools, buses and public facilities.

data.targetWord: laws and customs in the southern United States that enforced racial segregation and discrimination after the abolition of slavery

examples.en-GB: Jim Crow laws denied Black Americans equal access to schools, restaurants and voting booths.

data.targetWord: refusing to buy goods, use services or support an organisation in order to create pressure for change

examples.en-GB: The Montgomery Bus Boycott saw Black residents refuse to use city buses for over a year.

data.targetWord: protest that directly challenges an unfair system, such as sit-ins, marches, occupations or refusing to follow unjust rules

examples.en-GB: Sit-in protesters used direct action to challenge segregated lunch counters in the American South.

data.targetWord: a carefully planned form of protest that avoids physical violence but can be active, disruptive and dangerous for participants

examples.en-GB: Martin Luther King Jr argued for non-violent protest, training marchers to respond calmly to abuse.

data.targetWord: ordinary people organising locally within affected communities to create change from below

examples.en-GB: Grassroots activists organised car pools, raised funds and kept the Montgomery Bus Boycott going for over a year.

data.targetWord: a system of racial segregation and white minority rule in South Africa, in place from 1948 to the early 1990s

examples.en-GB: Under apartheid, Black South Africans were denied equal rights in housing, voting and employment.

data.targetWord: unfair treatment of a person or group because of characteristics such as race, sex, disability or religion

examples.en-GB: Race Relations Acts in Britain made racial discrimination unlawful in public places, housing and employment.

data.targetWord: laws made by Parliament or another law-making body that can change rights and protections

examples.en-GB: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 was landmark legislation that banned segregation in many public places.

data.targetWord: bringing people of different races together into shared schools, public spaces and institutions instead of keeping them separated

examples.en-GB: After the Brown v Board ruling, schools in the United States were supposed to move towards integration.

data.targetWord: a civil rights activist whose arrest in Montgomery, Alabama in 1955 for refusing to give up her bus seat helped trigger the Montgomery Bus Boycott

examples.en-GB: Rosa Parks was an experienced activist, not simply a tired passenger who refused to move.

data.targetWord: a minister and civil rights leader who argued for non-violent protest and became one of the most prominent figures in the American civil rights movement

examples.en-GB: Martin Luther King Jr delivered his 'I Have a Dream' speech at the March on Washington in 1963.

data.targetWord: the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, founded in 1909, which used legal action and campaigning to challenge racism in the United States

examples.en-GB: The NAACP supported families in the Brown v Board of Education case that challenged school segregation.

data.targetWord: a landmark 1954 US Supreme Court ruling that declared segregated public schools unconstitutional

examples.en-GB: Brown v Board showed that legal challenges could create change, though school desegregation still met resistance.

data.targetWord: a major United States law that banned segregation in public places and prohibited employment discrimination based on race, colour, religion, sex or national origin

examples.en-GB: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 was a major achievement after years of campaigning and protest.

data.targetWord: a 1963 protest in Bristol against the bus company's colour bar that prevented Black and Asian workers from being employed as bus crews

examples.en-GB: The Bristol Bus Boycott helped expose racial discrimination in British employment and influenced later Race Relations legislation.

data.targetWord: a policy or practice of refusing employment, service or access to people on the basis of their skin colour

examples.en-GB: Bristol's bus company operated a colour bar that prevented Black and Asian men from becoming bus drivers or conductors.

data.targetWord: British laws passed in 1965, 1968 and 1976 that progressively banned racial discrimination in public places, housing, employment and services

examples.en-GB: The Race Relations Acts showed that protest and pressure could lead to protective legislation in Britain.

data.targetWord: a British law that made it unlawful to pay men and women differently for doing equal work, though enforcement was gradual

examples.en-GB: The Equal Pay Act followed the 1968 Ford Dagenham sewing machinists' strike for fair wages.

data.targetWord: an anti-apartheid leader who was imprisoned for 27 years and became South Africa's first Black president in 1994 after the end of apartheid

examples.en-GB: Nelson Mandela's release from prison in 1990 was a symbol of the beginning of the end of apartheid.

data.targetWord: a form of direct action in which protesters occupy a space — such as a segregated lunch counter — and refuse to leave until demands are met

examples.en-GB: The Greensboro sit-ins of 1960 saw students challenge segregated lunch counters across the American South.

data.targetWord: using courts and the law to challenge unfair rules or practices and seek change through judicial decisions

examples.en-GB: The NAACP used legal challenges to argue that segregated schools violated the US Constitution.

data.targetWord: a British law that brought together many equality protections and prohibited discrimination based on race, sex, disability, religion and other characteristics

examples.en-GB: The Equality Act 2010 consolidated previous anti-discrimination laws into a single comprehensive piece of legislation.

data.targetWord: a United States law that protected the voting rights of Black Americans by addressing barriers such as literacy tests and intimidation used in southern states

examples.en-GB: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 gave federal government power to enforce Black voting rights in states where they had been denied.

data.sentence: Rosa Parks was arrested in ____ in 1955, helping to trigger the Montgomery Bus Boycott.
The 1954 ____ ruling declared that segregated public schools were unconstitutional in the USA.
The ____ of 1964 banned segregation in many public places in the USA and prohibited employment discrimination.
The 1963 ____ challenged a colour bar preventing Black and Asian workers from becoming bus drivers.
____ was a system of racial segregation and white minority rule in South Africa from 1948 to the early 1990s.
Nelson Mandela became South Africa's first Black president in ____ after the end of apartheid.
The ____ sit-ins of 1960 were an example of direct action against segregated lunch counters.
Britain's first Race Relations Act was passed in ____, banning racial discrimination in some public places.
The 1968 Ford Dagenham sewing machinists' ____ helped draw attention to unequal pay for women.
Non-violent protest was not ____; marchers trained carefully and expected arrest or violence.
Martin Luther King Jr gave his 'I Have a Dream' speech at the ____ in 1963.
The Voting Rights Act of ____ protected Black Americans' voting rights in southern states.
The ____ Act 2010 brought together many British equality laws and protected people from discrimination based on multiple characteristics.
An economic argument for the success of the Montgomery Bus Boycott was that Black passengers made up a large part of the bus company's ____.
Ella Baker and Jo Ann Robinson showed that civil rights campaigns depended on ____ activists, not just famous leaders.
Many migrants from the Caribbean faced signs saying 'No Blacks, No ____, No Dogs' in boarding houses across Britain.
International pressure on South Africa included economic ____, sporting bans and cultural campaigns against apartheid.

data.title: Order the key events of the US Civil Rights Movement
items: 1954 — Brown v Board of Education rules segregated schools unconstitutional
1955 — Rosa Parks arrested; Montgomery Bus Boycott begins
1960 — Greensboro sit-ins challenge segregated lunch counters
1963 — March on Washington; Martin Luther King Jr delivers 'I Have a Dream'
1964 — Civil Rights Act bans segregation and employment discrimination

data.title: Order the development of civil rights legislation in Britain
items: 1963 — Bristol Bus Boycott challenges colour bar in employment
1965 — First Race Relations Act bans discrimination in some public places
1968 — Race Relations Act extended to housing and employment
1970 — Equal Pay Act makes unequal pay for equal work unlawful
2010 — Equality Act brings together multiple anti-discrimination protections

data.title: Order the key events in the struggle against apartheid
items: 1948 — Apartheid becomes official policy in South Africa
1960s–1980s — International boycotts, sanctions and sporting bans grow
1994 — South Africa holds first fully democratic elections; Mandela becomes president
